India’s GCC ecosystem employs around 2.4 million people, and they are adding roughly 1.2 lakh new roles this year. 

But, they have also laid off around 5,000-30,000 people till now this year.

The layoffs are primarily of the roles that can easily be replaced by AI like document processing, basic data entry, and repetitive compliance checks.

And the roles they’re hiring for are more client-facing work, where there’s a requirement of having judgement that AI doesn’t have.

It’s just the start, in the coming times we will see more companies and sectors do this because every sector has roles that can be easily automated by AI (most of the entry level roles).

Why Your Sales Team Needs a Munshi, Not a Manager

Issue #4 — MANUFACTURING REVENUE SYSTEM by Rajnish Sharma

**Your sales manager is paid ₹1.5 lakhs/month to do a job that doesn't exist.**

I say this after 35 years in manufacturing and hiring dozens of "sales heads."

Here's what actually happens: You bring in someone with a fancy resume. They create spreadsheets. They attend meetings. They give you weekly updates about "pipeline momentum." Three months later, you're still losing deals to competitors who move faster.

The leak isn't in your sales team. It's in your systems.

**What a Manager Does (And Why It's Not Enough)**

A traditional sales manager optimizes for activity metrics:
- Calls made
- Meetings scheduled
- Proposals sent
- Deal closure rate

These are vanity numbers in MSME manufacturing. What you actually need is **deal velocity acceleration** — moving from lead to contract faster than your competition.

Managers manage people. They motivate. They measure. But they don't *engineer* the sales process itself.

When was the last time your sales head analyzed *why* a deal took 45 days instead of 15? When did he systematize the follow-up sequence after a quotation? Who's tracking that crucial 3-day window after technical approval when decision-makers go quiet?

Spoiler: Nobody. That's your pipeline leak.

**Enter the Munshi Mindset**

A "Munshi" (in the original sense) was India's accounting backbone — meticulous, systematic, detail-obsessed. In modern sales operations, you need someone who thinks like one.

What's different:

A manager asks: "Why didn't Sharma close the Kelvinator deal?"
A Munshi asks: "On Day 8 after quotation, why wasn't there a technical clarification call? Who owns that step?"

A manager tracks: "We sent 120 quotations this month."
A Munshi tracks: "Of those 120, only 40 got technical follow-up. The other 80 died silently."

A manager sets targets: "Close ₹50 lakhs this quarter."
A Munshi builds the system: "With 8 quotations per week and 35% conversion, we'll hit ₹52 lakhs. Here's the exact sequence to protect that 35%."

**Real Data from Manufacturing**

Most MSME sales teams lose 55-60% of qualified leads between quotation and closure. That's not a sales problem. That's a process problem.

We analyzed 847 deals across 34 manufacturing clients. The difference between closers and non-closers wasn't personality or pitch quality. It was **systematic follow-up discipline**:

- Deals with 3+ scheduled touchpoints post-quotation: 64% closure rate
- Deals with ad-hoc follow-up: 28% closure rate

That's a 2.3x difference. And it's entirely predictable.

Your sales head didn't know this was happening because he was in meetings, not in the weeds.

**What MUNSHI AI Does Differently**

At MUNSHI AI, we've built AI systems that think like operational Munshis, not salespeople.

Rakesh, our Head of Operations Implementation, saw this firsthand with a ball bearing manufacturer in Bangalore.

The Forward Deployed Engineer might be the most important AI job nobody explained properly.
It's not a solutions architect. The SA sells the dream. The FDE makes it real — embedded inside the customer's environment, shipping production AI after the contract is signed.
Why it's exploding:
• Job postings jumped 729% year over year — 643 in April 2025 to 5,330 in April 2026 (Indeed data)
• ~95% of enterprise GenAI pilots deliver no measurable business impact (MIT NANDA) — the failure is deployment, not the model
• Median base around $174K, with frontier labs paying far more in total comp
What the job actually is: part engineer, part consultant, part product manager. You map real workflows, build pipelines and integrations, ship agents and RAG systems, run evals, debug production incidents, and feed field lessons back into the product. Palantir calls it being the "startup CTO for the engagement."
The skill profile is T-shaped: Python, SQL/Spark, cloud, RAG, agentic orchestration like LangGraph, evals and guardrails — plus customer empathy, ownership, and comfort with messy, undocumented reality. FDEs reportedly spend about 47% of their week customer-facing.
The gap is the opportunity: companies are hiring for FDE capabilities faster than professionals understand the role. If you can sit with a customer, unpack a real problem, and make the technology work in practice — that's the job.

• Action: Re-skill around niche domains—Agentic AI, Cloud FinOps, Core R&D, and Cybersecurity. Build career paths rooted in subject-matter authority, not just people management.
👉 You’re stuck if: Your senior leaders’ main KPI is span of control.

⚙️ Layer 3: Agentic Workflows & Tech Stack (The Productivity Multiplier)
• The Shift: Stop measuring throughput purely by FTE hours.
• Action: Embed AI-native tools and automated governance across engineering and ops. Move your core metric from headcount growth to Total Value of Ownership (TVO): business outcomes delivered against investment.
👉 You’re stuck if: Your growth plan is still just a hiring plan.

🤝 Layer 4: Ecosystem & Partner Consolidation (The Operating Model)
• The Shift: Eliminate vendor bloat and tail providers.
• Action: Carve out transactional, non-core work to strategic partners via BOT or managed services on outcome-based contracts. Keep core IP and strategic capabilities strictly in-house.
👉 You’re stuck if: You manage dozens of vendors but can’t name the outcome each one owns.

---

📍 Where to start, by Avatar (ref Part 2):
• Strategic Innovation Hub: Focus on Layers 1 & 3. Formalize ownership, then multiply output.
• Rationalized Asset: Focus on Layers 4 & 1. Carve out non-core, redefine what stays.
• Lean-Start GCC: Build all four from Day 1—designing them in beats retrofitting later.

💡 Why all four must move together:
Transform talent (Layer 2) without fixing the mandate (Layer 1), and your best people will leave. Add AI (Layer 3) without streamlining your partner ecosystem (Layer 4), and you simply automate existing inefficiencies.

---

Everyone wants an experienced Project Architect, Contract Administrator or Project Manager, but if we stop investing in people at the beginning of their careers, where will that experience come from?

AI is adding a new dimension to that question.
SEEK’s September 2026 research challenges the assumption that junior roles will be the first to disappear. Across the Australian knowledge-based occupations studied, the stronger signal was that AI helping people perform tasks was associated with a growing share of early-career job ads. The effect linked to task automation was smaller and negative.

That doesn’t prove AI is creating jobs, or establish a hiring trend specifically for architecture and construction, but it gives employers a reason to question the “AI means fewer juniors” narrative.

The shift is already visible in architectural practice.
The Association of Consulting Architects’ 2026 survey found 70% of responding Australian practices use AI occasionally, regularly or through integrated workflows. Yet 68% have no formal AI policy.
Meanwhile, RICS’ global construction research identified a lack of skilled personnel as the most commonly reported barrier to AI adoption.

Our take? This is as much a people-development challenge as a technology decision. Consider an architecture graduate using AI to explore a concept or a junior Contract Administrator using it to prepare a first draft of project correspondence.

Producing an output faster doesn’t demonstrate that they understand the design constraints, contractual context or consequences of getting it wrong.
That understanding needs deliberate development.

For employers, three priorities stand out:
• Hire for reasoning. Ask candidates to explain their decisions, check an output and identify what needs further investigation.
• Protect learning opportunities. Keep juniors involved in site visits, coordination meetings, drawing reviews and commercial discussions.
• Give AI use a framework. Set clear expectations around approved tools, confidential information and senior review.

AI may change the tasks that start a career. We still need to build the experience that sustains one.

Most "AI automation" advice has the same subtext: buy another platform. For most small businesses, that's the wrong answer.

 Here's what actually holds businesses back — it isn't a lack of tools. You already have email, a CRM, Xero or MYOB, a booking form. The problem is they don't talk to each other, so a person ends up being the integration layer: copying a name from one system, pasting it into the next, updating the same detail in three places.
That manual "glue work" is exactly what automation removes. Not by replacing people, and not by adding another subscription — simply by getting the tools you already pay for to hand information across. An enquiry arrives and lands where it needs to, without anyone re-typing it.
The part that matters, especially for anyone handling client data: done properly, automation isn't reckless. Low-risk, repetitive steps can run on their own. But anything touching money, a contract, or customer data should still pass a human check before it goes out. Efficiency and control aren't opposites — good automation keeps both.
So before hiring another admin or committing to a new platform, it's worth auditing what you already have. Nine times out of ten, the win isn't more tools. It's making the existing ones work together.
What's the one manual, copy-paste task in your business you'd automate first?

- Notion for documentation
- Box for stored files

But installing a plugin doesn't automatically connect your accounts.

You still need to configure and authorize each connector.

For example, different specialists could support research, analysis, or documentation.

Finance for reporting and reconciliation.

Data for cleaning, analysis, and dashboards.

Operations for processes and compliance.

10 December.
From that date, if software plays a real part in deciding who gets through your hiring process, your privacy policy has to say so.

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) released its guidance on 30 September. It reads the new rules broadly.
 - The software doesn’t have to make the decision. It only has to play a substantial part in it.
 - A manager making the final call doesn’t take it out of scope.

CV screening and candidate ranking tools are the obvious ones to check. The harder ones are the features vendors have added since you signed the contract.

Our Salary Guide asked how far AI is embedded in organisations.
 - Just 8.3% have it fully embedded, with clear guidelines and approved tools. 
 - Another 16% say guidance exists but isn’t enforced.

So most organisations are about to be asked something they haven’t worked out yet:
 - Which tools touch our hiring decisions?
 - What do they do with candidate information?

We’re recruiters, not lawyers. Your legal team owns these answers.

Some businesses are telling the Fed that AI is changing how many people they hire.

The Federal Reserve put out its Beige Book on October 14. It's a regular report on conditions across the Fed's twelve Districts, pulled from interviews and questionnaires with businesses, community organizations, economists and other contacts. This time, five Districts reported that some firms had reduced staffing through attrition, delayed hiring, or expected less job creation after AI investments raised their productivity.

Two District reports stood out to me. In the Minneapolis District, IT staffing contacts said AI "was not causing layoffs but was dampening the creation of new jobs." In the Dallas District, an accounting contact said some large accounting firms are delaying new employment contracts because they may not need as many entry level employees as they first expected, partly because of efficiency gains from AI.

Let me be clear about what this is and what it isn't. The Beige Book is mostly qualitative. It's what contacts are saying, not a count. It doesn't tell us how many jobs are involved. And most Districts described little or no net change in overall employment. So nobody should read this as AI wiping out work.

Here's my read. Entry level work is how a lot of people get in the door. It's where you learn the job. If firms thin out that layer, the people who feel it are the ones just starting out. They won't show up in a layoff headline. They'll just hear "we're not hiring right now."

That's why AGI Affinity exists. We help organizations get their people ready for AI, from awareness to mastery. If the first rung gets thinner, people need to be ready for the next one. No one gets left behind.

Source: Federal Reserve, "Beige Book, October 2026," National Summary, with links to the Minneapolis and Dallas District reports, October 14, 2026.

The IPAF Summit in Istanbul revealed a paradox about AI and the people who run equipment rental depots.

95% of the delegates said the depot manager, not the AI, should decide when a customer disputes damage on a returned machine. 76% said that if AI handled the paperwork, they would hire fewer juniors. Another 9% said they already have.

Francesco Marini and I put both questions to a room of people from the powered access rental industry, during our workshop on practical uses of AI. We covered a lot in almost an hour, from documents and pricing to damage inspections and robots on platforms. These two answers, a few minutes apart, are the ones I keep coming back to.

Each answer makes sense on its own. Put them side by side and there is a gap.

In equipment rental, the depot manager is the person who knows which machine can go out to which site, what condition it came back in, and when a scratch matters less than a customer of fifteen years. Nobody learns that on a course. You learn it by spending years in the yard and at the hire desk next to someone who already knows, and very often you start from the paperwork: delivery notes, inspection reports, contracts. And when we asked the room to rank ten possible uses of AI in their business, training new staff came last.

So the question we closed the workshop with is still open: if AI does the junior’s paperwork, who will be your depot manager in 2040?

I see three possible paths for the industry.
1. Rental companies hire fewer juniors, save on admin, and discover in 2040 that nobody has learned the trade. Then they will be poaching depot managers from each other.
2. Rental companies keep hiring juniors, give the paperwork to AI, and put those juniors closer to the real decisions sooner: at the hire desk, in the yard, at the check-in of a returned machine. AI becomes the tutor that is still there at eight in the evening, when the senior has gone home.
3. Before their most experienced people retire, rental companies write down what those people know about their machines, customers and sites, so AI can carry it to whoever comes next. The understanding stays with people. AI just stops it from walking out of the door.

The first path is the one an industry drifts into without deciding. The other two have to be chosen, and every rental company should make that choice now.

Thank you International Powered Access Federation (IPAF) for hosting us and for the photos, and to everyone in the room who joined the discussion.

Recruitment scam, Part 2: how I confirmed it, and the red flags you can catch early. (Part 1 is in the comments.)
A quick reality check showed it was a 100% scam:
1. The studio's name. No website, no reviews, nothing about the studio itself. Only Google's AI overview flagging it as part of a known "recruiter-to-resume-writer" LinkedIn scam, and a couple of Reddit threads describing the same scheme.
2. The recruiter's profile. Created that same month, yet listing a career back to 2008 at generic-sounding agencies. No verification, no contact details.
3. The writing. When I hesitated over the price, the recruiter and the studio asked me to name a "comfortable" amount within moments of each other. Both also shared a verbal tic: requests opening with "Kindly...". Most likely one operator behind both chats.
I simply sent them the AI overview screenshot and closed both chats. LinkedIn flagged the chat as harmful within minutes, and the recruiter's profile was gone soon after.
Looking back, though, the warning signs were there long before that check. The "hiring process" showed almost every scam red flag in the book, many of them from the very first message:
• A vacancy description covering every location, every work format and every contract type at once
• Overall, requirements so generic they would fit almost any developer
• A salary far above market and a promised fast track to lead roles
• "Just reply with the word 'interested'": fishing for people who won't ask questions
• A sudden "low ATS score" with "proof" nobody can read
• A referral to one specific paid service, with ready instructions on how to reach it and a word-for-word script for the first message
• A hard deadline (6 hours) and constant check-ins
• The conversation moving to another messenger
• Heavy use of abbreviations, both real (CPRW, iCIMS) and made-up (P.A.C.E., CPOM)
• A "certified" team pasting raw, unformatted AI output
• A negotiable price: "what amount would be comfortable for you?"
• Any request for your login or password
In conclusion, a few habits that will make your job search both safer and more productive:
• Find out who is actually hiring: a product company, a recruitment agency or an outstaffing company. A missing employer name alone isn't a red flag, as agencies often can't name the client early. But a real recruiter can at least describe the company type, industry and product.
• Check the recruiter: profile age, history, mutual connections, and whether their agency exists.
• Once you know the employer, look for the role on the company's own careers page.
• Google every company, service and name you are given. It takes 30 seconds.
And remember: real recruiters are paid by companies, not candidates. Anyone between you and a job who asks for money or credentials is not part of a real hiring process.

AI-led interviews are moving from pilot to production for high-volume hiring. Before anyone signs a vendor contract, a PM should be asking one thing: who owns this?

I'd treat it like any other implementation brief. Before the pilot starts, get clear on:

✅ Success metrics: time-to-screen, drop-off rate, quality of hire. Not just speed.
✅ Human fallback: what happens when a candidate opts out or the AI gets it wrong?
✅ Audit evidence: can you show how scores were produced and tested for bias?
✅ Candidate experience: how will you measure it, and who acts on the results?

Faster screening is easy to sell. Defensible screening is the harder deliverable.
